title: Bad circumstances as the path
hook: third point: turn difficulties into practice

segments.voice: Yesterday, sending and taking: in with the heavy, out with the light. Your line was riding the breath. Did you breathe once for someone having a hard time? Day one thousand two hundred ninety-nine.

The board flips from delayed to canceled. A groan goes down the gate area. Somebody is already shouting at the agent, who didn't cancel anything. Your phone is at nine percent. The next flight is tomorrow. In that moment there are two stories available. In one, the day has been ruined and the path, whatever you were practicing, is on hold until life calms down. In the other, this gate, this groan, this nine percent is the path. Point three of the seven points of mind training picks the second story, on purpose. Today, bad circumstances as the path.
screen: `DELAYED. THEN CANCELED.` → `TWO STORIES AVAILABLE.` → `POINT THREE PICKS THE SECOND.`

segments.voice: First, the slogan that opens point three. In effect: when the world is full of trouble, turn every mishap into the path of awakening. Not after the trouble passes. Through it. A bad day isn't a break from practice. It's the material. Second, where the blame goes. Another slogan says to drive all blame into one. That one isn't the agent, and it isn't you as a person to be beaten up. In the commentaries, it's self-cherishing, the me-first reflex that turns every delay into a personal insult. The trouble may be real. The commentaries trace the extra misery to that reflex, and the slogan points the finger there. Third, gratitude, of all things. Another slogan says to be grateful to everyone. The commentaries explain it this way: a person who tests your patience gives you a chance to practice patience that an easy person never could. A story told about Atisha says he brought a difficult, short-tempered attendant with him to Tibet, and when asked why, called him his teacher of patience. Fourth, what this is not. It isn't a teaching to stay where you're being harmed, or to call injustice fine. You can leave the gate, rebook, speak up. Point three is about the mind that goes with you while you do. Yesterday's tonglen fits right in here: breathe in the frustration of the whole gate area, breathe out a little patience toward everyone stuck with you, including the agent.
screen: `TURN EVERY MISHAP INTO THE PATH.` · `DRIVE ALL BLAME INTO ONE.` · `BE GRATEFUL TO EVERYONE.` · `NOT A TEACHING TO STAY IN HARM.` · then, large: `TROUBLE IS THE PATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: use one annoyance as practice. Sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind a small annoyance from the last day or two, not a big wound, just a splinter. Let it play once. Notice where the me-first reflex shows up: why me, how dare they. Then try two moves from point three. Point the blame at that reflex instead of at the person. And look for one thing the annoyance is teaching, patience, slowing down, anything. Breathe with it until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Bad circumstances as the path. The third of the seven points: trouble isn't an interruption of practice; it's the practice. Today's word.
screen: `BAD CIRCUMSTANCES AS THE PATH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: trouble is the path. Today, the next time something small goes wrong, say the line to yourself before you say anything else. Day one thousand two hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Practitioners of Tibetan mind training use the slogans of point three in daily life, treating setbacks, illness and difficult people as occasions to practice patience, compassion and letting go of self-cherishing.

myth: point three says to wait until life calms down to practice
it says to turn every mishap into the path, through the trouble, not after it.
drive all blame into one means beat yourself up
the commentaries point the blame at self-cherishing, not at you as a person.
a story says Atisha called a difficult attendant his teacher of patience
a story told about him; the point is that difficult people give patience a chance.

fork.setup: your flight is canceled. the gate area groans. someone is shouting at the agent. what does point three suggest?
options: treat this as the practice, and breathe patience toward everyone stuck.
pretend everything is fine and feel nothing.
fork.reveal: point three turns mishaps into the path. you can still rebook and speak up; the practice is the mind you bring with you.

original.note: Tibetan lam, path, the same lam as in lamrim, the stages of the path.

trapdoor: what you thought: look on the bright side.
what it means: point three of mind training: trouble isn't a break from practice but its material, with blame pointed at self-cherishing.
what a scholar hears: slogans like 'drive all blame into one' and 'be grateful to everyone' aim at the me-first reflex, not at denying that harm is real.
